findings.title: epoll EFAULT loses edge-triggered readiness
findings.summary: EpollFile::wait removes an edge-triggered ready entry before sys_epoll_wait copies it to user memory. If that copy faults, the syscall returns EFAULT but the ready edge is not restored, so a later valid epoll_wait sees no event. The bounded model reaches the lost-undelivered epoch in nine states and the public eventfd reproduction observes the missing redelivery in an SMP=2 Asterinas VM.
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 2 (same edge-triggered pre-copyout delivery-commit mechanism)

findings.title: epoll EFAULT disables one-shot interest before delivery
findings.summary: Entry::poll disables an EPOLLONESHOT observer when it observes readiness, before the selected event is copied to user memory. A copyout EFAULT therefore leaves an event that was never delivered permanently disabled until EPOLL_CTL_MOD. The ten-state model trace and the SMP=2 public eventfd test both show this behavior.
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 2 (same one-shot pre-copyout delivery-commit mechanism)

findings.title: final close leaves a dead epoll interest entry
findings.summary: The epoll key includes the weak file-object identity, preventing descriptor-number reuse from retargeting a watch, but final close has no immediate epoll cleanup hook. The dead weak entry remains in the interest set until a later ready-list scan notices it. The seven-state model trace is directly observable through a stale /proc/self/fdinfo entry in the SMP=2 VM test.
findings.dedup_note: also covers the epoll-key and final-close portions of code-review Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 (same weak-OFD identity and interest-cleanup mechanisms)

findings.title: consumed timerfd remains ready through the poll cache
findings.summary: Timerfd expiration invalidates and caches readiness, but a successful read clears ticks without invalidating the shared Pollee cache. A subsequent zero-timeout poll can report POLLIN even though the next read returns EAGAIN. The nine-state model trace and public timerfd reproduction both show stale readiness.
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 3 (same timerfd consumed-readiness cache-invalidation mechanism)

findings.title: signalfd mask update does not publish readiness
findings.summary: Updating an existing signalfd mask only stores the new mask. A signal that was already pending can become readable under that new mask without notifying the thread or process signal-queue poller registered by epoll. The temporal counterexample reaches the lost transition in eight states and the SMP=2 signalfd test times out instead of receiving the pending signal.
findings.dedup_note: also covers the mask-update notification portion of code-review Scenario 4 (same pending-signal transition mechanism)

findings.title: poll returns timeout after timerfd becomes readable
findings.summary: The timeout return path in do_poll does not rescan descriptors after the waiting primitive returns ETIME. A timerfd can increment its readable tick counter at the timeout boundary, yet poll returns zero; an immediate read then succeeds. The six-state model trace is reproduced in repeated SMP=2 timerfd stress runs.
findings.dedup_note: also covers the poll terminal-rescan portion of code-review Scenario 5 (same timeout/readiness arbitration mechanism)

findings.title: captured FD operations and exec cutover may lose OFD identity
findings.summary: Numeric FD slots can be reused while a captured operation, duplicated descriptor, or shared status remains attached to the original open file description (OFD). The reviewed lookup, replacement, deferred-cleanup, and close-on-exec paths must preserve that OFD identity rather than re-resolving the reused number. MC-3 covers the epoll-key and final-close portion of this scenario, but it does not cover captured-operation, duplication, or exec-cutover sites. Confirmation should exercise close/reuse, dup, and exec interleavings while checking slot identity separately from the captured OFD.

findings.title: signalfd epoll registration may bind readiness to the wrong thread
findings.summary: SignalFile::poll evaluates and registers signalfd readiness against the current thread, even though another thread may later wait on or read the shared descriptor. A signal pending for that waiter could make a direct signalfd read readable without waking the queue selected when epoll_ctl ran. MC-5 covers the distinct missing-notification path when an existing signalfd mask is updated, but it does not cover registration-thread versus wait-thread identity. Confirmation should use two threads that split epoll_ctl from epoll_wait or read and compare the wakeup with direct readability.

findings.title: epoll and mask-taking waits may bypass terminal readiness arbitration
findings.summary: The epoll, ppoll, pselect6, and epoll_pwait paths combine terminal timeout or signal selection with temporary signal-mask handling. Each path must rescan registered descriptors before returning and restore the saved mask on every terminal path. MC-6 covers the poll/timerfd timeout race, but it does not cover EpollFile::wait or the mask-taking syscall paths. Confirmation should race readiness, timeout, and signals on those paths and inspect both the return value and post-return signal mask.

findings.title: nested epoll cycle checks and synchronous callbacks may deadlock
findings.summary: EpollFile::add_interest accepts epoll targets without self or cycle validation, and readiness propagation invokes observers synchronously while ready-set and observer-set locks are held. A self-edge or two-epoll back-edge could create unsupported cyclic propagation or a lock-order cycle during callback delivery. This scenario was not model-checked and remains a candidate even though the current test suite blocklists cycle conformance. Confirmation should bound the graph to two epoll instances and separate unsupported topology from any failure of a supported acyclic path.
